svg.aria-label: Diagram: allocation quotas versus rate quotas in Google Cloud, the dimensions that decide where each is counted, the three enforcement levels, and the system limits that are neither and cannot be raised
svg.title: Google Cloud quotas: allocation versus rate, the dimensions that scope them, the enforcement levels, and system limits
svg.text: Two kinds of quota behind one word, and a third thing that is not a quota at all
One counts what exists. One counts how fast you ask. Only one of them has a clock attached.
Allocation quota — a level
Restricts how much of a resource Google Cloud allocates to you.
Also known as resource quotas.
Counts things that exist. Usage falls when you delete them
— and for some metrics, when you stop them.
No clock: the number is a level, not a rate.
Dimension is usually region or zone, plus product attributes
such as gpu_family.
Console Current usage: the most recent value.
quota/allocation/usage — chart as a stacked bar, a week wide.
Rate quota — a flow
Restricts the rate at which you can consume a resource.
Specifies a time period and an amount over that period.
Counts requests. Usage falls only when the period resets;
nothing you do makes it fall sooner.
Per-day resets at midnight Pacific Time. Per-minute resets
one minute after your first request, in a rolling window.
Refill is synchronised: reach it at 10:00:15 and it refills
at 10:01:00, not sixty seconds later.
quota/rate/net_usage — console shows a 10-minute average.
Neither is a single number: a dimension decides where the counting happens
Cloud Quotas dimensions represent different ways of measuring resource usage, and the API represents them as
key-value pairs: key region, value us-central1. Region and zone are the familiar ones; product attributes such as
gpu_family slice the same resource along a line that has nothing to do with geography.
So CPUs is not a quota. CPUs in us-central1 for project X is one. Regional quotas are not a subset of project quotas.
Enforcement level decides whose usage counts toward it
Project level
Restricts usage within one project.
Using the resource in one project
does not affect available quota in
another. The sane default.
Folder level
Restricts usage within a folder.
Child folders and projects
contribute to the usage, so one
project can fail another one.
Organization level
The same shape, one level up.
Child folders and projects
contribute to the usage.
A ceiling for a whole estate.
The third category: system limits, which are neither, and which cannot be raised
System limits are fixed constraints, such as maximum file sizes or database schema limitations, which cannot be
increased or decreased. Compute Engine lists them separately from resource quotas and from API rate quotas.
A concurrent operations limit counts operations in flight right now, not requests sent in the last minute — and it
returns the same 403 with reason rateLimitExceeded that a rate quota returns.
The remedy is backoff, client-side rate limiting and less short polling — never a larger number.
